questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He gave me many advices.
He gave me many advice.
He gave me much advice.
He gave me an advice.
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is an uncountable noun; it cannot take plural '-s' or 'many'. Say 'much advice' or 'many pieces of advice'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: All the furnitures were sold.
All the furniture was sold.
All the furniture were sold.
All furnitures was sold.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable singular noun; it takes singular verb 'was'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He bought three dozens bananas.
He bought three dozen bananas.
He bought three dozens of bananas.
He bought three dozen of bananas.
questions.explanation: When preceded by a definite numeral (three), 'dozen' does not take '-s': 'three dozen bananas'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: One of the student was absent.
One of the students was absent.
One of the students were absent.
One of student were absent.
questions.explanation: 'One of the' is followed by a plural noun ('students') and a singular verb ('was').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is senior than me.
He is senior to me.
He is more senior than me.
He is senior over me.
questions.explanation: Latin comparatives (senior, junior, superior, inferior) take 'to', not 'than'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I prefer coffee than tea.
I prefer coffee to tea.
I prefer coffee more than tea.
I prefer coffee over tea.
questions.explanation: 'Prefer' takes preposition 'to'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He told that he is unwell.
He said that he was unwell.
He said that he is unwell.
He told me that he is unwell.
questions.explanation: 'Told' requires an indirect object; in reported speech past principal clause requires past subordinate clause ('was unwell').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She is married with a doctor.
She is married to a doctor.
She is married by a doctor.
She got married with a doctor.
questions.explanation: In standard English, one is married 'to' someone, not 'with'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He entered into the classroom.
He entered the classroom.
He entered in the classroom.
He entered to the classroom.
questions.explanation: 'Enter' (physical entry) is a transitive verb that does not take preposition 'into'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: We discussed about the problem.
We discussed the problem.
We discussed on the problem.
We discussed over the problem.
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' means talk about, so adding 'about' is redundant.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She resembles to her mother.
She resembles with her mother.
She resembles her mother.
She resembles like her mother.
questions.explanation: 'Resemble' is a transitive verb that takes no preposition.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I have ordered for a cup of tea.
I ordered for a cup of tea.
I have ordered a cup of tea.
I have ordered to a cup of tea.
questions.explanation: 'Order' takes a direct object without preposition 'for'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The sceneries of Kashmir are charming.
The scenery of Kashmir is charming.
The sceneries of Kashmir is charming.
The scenery of Kashmir are charming.
questions.explanation: 'Scenery' is an uncountable singular noun; 'sceneries' does not exist in standard English.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He has black hairs.
He has black hair.
He has a black hair.
His hairs are black.
questions.explanation: Hair on the head is treated as uncountable singular: 'black hair'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The cattle is grazing in the field.
The cattles are grazing in the field.
The cattle are grazing in the field.
The cattles is grazing in the field.
questions.explanation: 'Cattle' is an inherently plural collective noun taking a plural verb ('are'), and cannot be pluralized as 'cattles'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The police has caught the thief.
The police have caught the thief.
The polices have caught the thief.
A police have caught the thief.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is plural in English, requiring plural verb 'have'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I met him two years ago.
I have met him two years ago.
I had met him two years ago.
I meet him two years ago.
questions.explanation: 'Ago' requires Simple Past tense ('met').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He has left for London yesterday.
He left for London yesterday.
He had left for London yesterday.
He leaves for London yesterday.
questions.explanation: Definite past time marker 'yesterday' requires Simple Past ('left').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: It is raining since morning.
It has been raining since morning.
It was raining since morning.
It had rained since morning.
questions.explanation: Action continuing up to present with 'since' requires Present Perfect Continuous ('has been raining').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is suffering from fever since three days.
He has been suffering from fever for three days.
He is suffering with fever for three days.
He was suffering from fever since three days.
questions.explanation: Duration takes 'for three days', and ongoing illness takes 'has been suffering from'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: If it will rain, we shall cancel the match.
If it rains, we shall cancel the match.
If it rain, we shall cancel the match.
If it would rain, we shall cancel the match.
questions.explanation: The 'if' clause in Type 1 conditionals uses Simple Present ('rains'), never 'will'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: If I had money, I would have bought the car.
If I had money, I would buy the car.
If I have money, I would buy the car.
If I had money, I will buy the car.
questions.explanation: Type 2 conditional: 'If + had' (Simple Past) -> 'would + buy'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: If he had worked hard, he would pass.
If he had worked hard, he would have passed.
If he worked hard, he would have passed.
If he had worked hard, he will pass.
questions.explanation: Type 3 conditional: 'If + had worked' -> 'would have passed'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Unless you do not work hard, you will fail.
Unless you work hard, you will fail.
Unless you will work hard, you will fail.
Unless you did not work hard, you will fail.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' already means 'if not'; do not use another negative 'do not' in the same clause.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Until he does not arrive, wait here.
Until he arrives, wait here.
Until he will arrive, wait here.
Until he arrived, wait here.
questions.explanation: 'Until' already contains a negative time limit; do not use 'does not'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He did not wrote the letter.
He did not write the letter.
He did not written the letter.
He not wrote the letter.
questions.explanation: Auxiliary 'did' is followed by the base form V1 ('write'), never past tense 'wrote'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Does he goes to school?
Does he go to school?
Does he went to school?
Does he going to school?
questions.explanation: Auxiliary 'does' is followed by base form 'go' without '-es'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is good in Mathematics.
He is good at Mathematics.
He is good with Mathematics.
He is good into Mathematics.
questions.explanation: Skill/proficiency in a subject takes preposition 'good at', not 'good in'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She is proficient at English.
She is proficient in English.
She is proficient with English.
She is proficient by English.
questions.explanation: 'Proficient' takes preposition 'in'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He died from cancer.
He died of cancer.
He died with cancer.
He died by cancer.
questions.explanation: Death from a specific disease takes 'died of', while death from an indirect cause (overwork/wound) takes 'died from'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He was prevented to go there.
He was prevented from going there.
He was prevented of going there.
He was prevented against going there.
questions.explanation: 'Prevented' takes 'from + gerund' ('from going').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I insist to pay the bill.
I insist on paying the bill.
I insist for paying the bill.
I insist in paying the bill.
questions.explanation: 'Insist' takes preposition 'on + gerund' ('insist on paying').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is confident to win the match.
He is confident of winning the match.
He is confident for winning the match.
He is confident in winning the match.
questions.explanation: 'Confident' takes 'of + gerund' ('confident of winning').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She congratulated him for his success.
She congratulated him on his success.
She congratulated him at his success.
She congratulated him with his success.
questions.explanation: 'Congratulate' takes preposition 'on', never 'for'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He was accused for theft.
He was accused of theft.
He was accused with theft.
He was accused in theft.
questions.explanation: 'Accused' takes preposition 'of', never 'for'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I agree with your proposal.
I agree to your proposal.
I agree for your proposal.
I agree on your proposal.
questions.explanation: You agree 'with' a person, but agree 'to' a proposal/plan/terms.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I agree to you on this matter.
I agree with you on this matter.
I agree for you on this matter.
I agree by you on this matter.
questions.explanation: Agree 'with' a person: 'agree with you'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He parted with his friend with tears.
He parted from his friend with tears.
He parted to his friend with tears.
He parted by his friend with tears.
questions.explanation: You part 'from' a person, but part 'with' a possession/thing.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He refused to part from his wealth.
He refused to part with his wealth.
He refused to part of his wealth.
He refused to part for his wealth.
questions.explanation: Part 'with' property/wealth: 'part with his wealth'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Neither Rahul nor Rohit were present.
Neither Rahul nor Rohit was present.
Neither Rahul or Rohit was present.
Neither Rahul nor Rohit are present.
questions.explanation: When two singular subjects are joined by 'neither... nor', the verb is singular ('was').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Neither the teacher nor the students was present.
Neither the teacher nor the students were present.
Neither the teacher or the students were present.
Neither the teacher nor the students is present.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the closer subject ('students' -> 'were').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Either he or I are responsible.
Either he or I am responsible.
Either he or I is responsible.
Either he or I were responsible.
questions.explanation: The verb agrees with the nearer pronoun ('I' -> 'am').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Each of the boys have a pen.
Each of the boys has a pen.
Each of the boy has a pen.
Each of boys have a pen.
questions.explanation: 'Each of the boys' takes singular verb 'has'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Every one of the players have done their best.
Every one of the players has done his best.
Every one of the player has done his best.
Every one of the players have done his best.
questions.explanation: 'Every one' is singular, taking singular verb 'has' and singular pronoun 'his'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Many a man have died of malaria.
Many a man has died of malaria.
Many a men has died of malaria.
Many a men have died of malaria.
questions.explanation: 'Many a' is followed by a singular countable noun and singular verb: 'Many a man has died'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: More than one boy was absent.
More than one boys was absent.
More than one boy were absent.
More than one boys were absent.
questions.explanation: 'More than one' + singular noun takes a singular verb: 'More than one boy was absent'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Ten miles are a long distance to walk.
Ten miles is a long distance to walk.
Ten miles were a long distance to walk.
Ten mile is a long distance to walk.
questions.explanation: A definite distance/sum of money considered as a single unit takes a singular verb ('is').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Fifty thousand rupees were paid to him.
Fifty thousand rupees was a huge amount.
Fifty thousand rupees were a huge amount.
Fifty thousands rupees was a huge amount.
questions.explanation: When the sum represents a singular collective concept ('a huge amount'), it takes 'was'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Bread and butter are my favourite breakfast.
Bread and butter is my favourite breakfast.
Bread and butter were my favourite breakfast.
Breads and butter is my favourite breakfast.
questions.explanation: Two items expressing a single compound dish/idea take a singular verb ('is').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Slow and steady win the race.
Slow and steady wins the race.
Slow and steady are winning the race.
Slow and steady is winning the race.
questions.explanation: Proverb: 'Slow and steady wins the race'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The captain with his team members have arrived.
The captain with his team members has arrived.
The captain along his team members has arrived.
The captain as well as team members have arrived.
questions.explanation: With connecting phrases like 'with', 'along with', 'as well as', the verb agrees with the first subject ('The captain' -> 'has').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He as well as his friends are guilty.
He as well as his friends is guilty.
He as well as his friends were guilty.
He as well his friends is guilty.
questions.explanation: Subject 'He' governs the verb: 'is guilty'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He gave me a ten-rupees note.
He gave me a ten-rupee note.
He gave me an ten-rupee note.
He gave me ten-rupees note.
questions.explanation: When a numeral + noun acts as a hyphenated compound adjective before a noun, the hyphenated noun remains singular: 'a ten-rupee note'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She stayed in a five-stars hotel.
She stayed in a five-star hotel.
She stayed in five-star hotel.
She stayed in five-stars hotel.
questions.explanation: Compound adjective remains singular: 'five-star hotel'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He works very hardly.
He works very hard.
He hardly works very.
He is working hardly.
questions.explanation: 'Hard' is both adjective and adverb; 'hardly' means scarcely/almost not at all.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I could not scarcely hear his voice.
I could scarcely hear his voice.
I could not scarcely heard his voice.
I could scarcely not hear his voice.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely' is already semi-negative; using 'not' creates an erroneous double negative.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She is more taller than her sister.
She is taller than her sister.
She is much taller to her sister.
She is more tall than her sister.
questions.explanation: Double comparative ('more taller') is an error; use 'taller'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: This is the most unique monument in India.
This is a unique monument in India.
This is the unique monument in India.
This is a most unique monument in India.
questions.explanation: 'Unique' expresses an absolute state and cannot be qualified by comparative/superlative 'most'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He has no any friends in the city.
He has no friends in the city.
He has not friends in the city.
He has none friends in the city.
questions.explanation: 'No' and 'any' cannot be used together; say 'no friends' or 'not any friends'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He returned back yesterday.
He returned yesterday.
He returned back to home yesterday.
He did return back yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Return' already means to come back; adding 'back' is redundant.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Please repeat it again.
Please repeat it.
Please repeat again.
Please repeat it once again.
questions.explanation: 'Repeat' means to say/do again; 'repeat again' is redundant.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is my cousin brother.
He is my cousin.
He is cousin brother of mine.
He is my own cousin brother.
questions.explanation: The word 'cousin' does not take 'brother' or 'sister' in standard English.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I am giving an examination tomorrow.
I am taking an examination tomorrow.
I am appearing an examination tomorrow.
I am writing down an examination tomorrow.
questions.explanation: In English, a student 'takes' an exam, while the teacher/examiner 'gives' or conducts it.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Open your book at page fifty.
Open your book on page fifty.
Open your book in page fifty.
Open your book to page fifty.
questions.explanation: Specific page reference takes preposition 'at': 'at page fifty'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He sat under the shade of a tree.
He sat in the shade of a tree.
He sat on the shade of a tree.
He sat below the shade of a tree.
questions.explanation: One sits 'under a tree', but 'in the shade of a tree'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: What is the time in your watch?
What is the time by your watch?
What is the time on your watch?
What is the time with your watch?
questions.explanation: Time according to a timepiece is expressed as 'by your watch'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He wrote the letter with ink.
He wrote the letter in ink.
He wrote the letter by ink.
He wrote the letter on ink.
questions.explanation: A pen/pencil takes 'with a pen', but the medium of ink/pencil takes 'in ink' or 'in pencil'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He signed the document with pencil.
He signed the document in pencil.
He signed the document by pencil.
He signed the document on pencil.
questions.explanation: Substance medium takes 'in pencil'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He hanged his coat on the hook.
He hung his coat on the hook.
He has hanged his coat on the hook.
He was hung his coat on the hook.
questions.explanation: 'Hung' is the past of hang (suspending an object); 'hanged' is used exclusively for execution by hanging.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The murderer was hung yesterday.
The murderer was hanged yesterday.
The murderer hung yesterday.
The murderer is hanged yesterday.
questions.explanation: Execution by hanging takes 'hanged': 'The murderer was hanged yesterday'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He laid on the grass and fell asleep.
He lay on the grass and fell asleep.
He lied on the grass and fell asleep.
He was laid on the grass and fell asleep.
questions.explanation: Past tense of intransitive 'lie' (to recline) is 'lay'; 'laid' is transitive (to place something down).

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He laid the baby gently on the bed.
He lay the baby gently on the bed.
He lied the baby gently on the bed.
He was lying the baby on the bed.
questions.explanation: Past of transitive 'lay' (to put down) is 'laid'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The ship was drowned in the ocean.
The ship sank in the ocean.
The ship was sinking down in the ocean.
The ship drowned into the ocean.
questions.explanation: Non-living objects 'sink' (sank); living beings 'drown'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The boy sank in the river.
The boy drowned in the river.
The boy was sunk in the river.
The boy had sank in the river.
questions.explanation: Living humans and animals 'drown': 'The boy drowned in the river'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I have been to Delhi before two years.
I went to Delhi two years ago.
I had been to Delhi before two years.
I have gone to Delhi two years ago.
questions.explanation: Past specific time takes Simple Past with 'ago'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He has disposed off his old car.
He has disposed of his old car.
He has disposed away his old car.
He has disposed out his old car.
questions.explanation: The correct phrasal verb is 'dispose of' (with a single 'f'), never 'dispose off'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She is very much happy.
She is very happy.
She is too much happy.
She is much happy.
questions.explanation: Positive degree adjectives take 'very': 'very happy'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I am very glad to meet you.
I am much glad to meet you.
I am too glad to meet you.
I am very much glad to meet you.
questions.explanation: Positive adjective takes 'very glad'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is too happy to see you.
He is very happy to see you.
He is so happy to see you.
He is too much happy to see you.
questions.explanation: 'Too' implies excess with a negative sense ('too weak to walk'); say 'very happy'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: It is a true fact.
It is a fact.
It is a real true fact.
It is a completely true fact.
questions.explanation: A 'fact' is inherently true; saying 'true fact' is a pleonasm/redundancy.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He gave me a free gift.
He gave me a gift.
He gave me a costless gift.
He gave me a free of cost gift.
questions.explanation: A 'gift' is by definition free; 'free gift' is redundant.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The reason why he failed is because he was lazy.
The reason why he failed is that he was lazy.
The reason why he failed is due to he was lazy.
The reason he failed because he was lazy.
questions.explanation: After 'The reason is...', use 'that', never 'because' or 'due to'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Although he was ill, but he attended the exam.
Although he was ill, yet he attended the exam.
Although he was ill, so he attended the exam.
Although he was ill, and he attended the exam.
questions.explanation: 'Although' is never paired with 'but'; use 'yet' or a comma.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He did not know who to ask.
He did not know whom to ask.
He did not know which to ask.
He did not know whoever to ask.
questions.explanation: Object of the verb 'ask' is objective pronoun 'whom'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Between you and I, he is a fraud.
Between you and me, he is a fraud.
Between you and myself, he is a fraud.
Between you and him, I am a fraud.
questions.explanation: Prepositions ('between') govern objective case pronouns: 'between you and me'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Let you and I do this work.
Let you and me do this work.
Let you and myself do this work.
Let we do this work.
questions.explanation: The verb 'let' is followed by objective case pronouns: 'Let you and me do this work'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: It is me who did it.
It is I who did it.
It is myself who did it.
It was me who did it.
questions.explanation: Formal English requires subjective complement after 'be': 'It is I who did it'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: It was him who helped me.
It was he who helped me.
It was himself who helped me.
It is him who helped me.
questions.explanation: Predicate nominative: 'It was he who helped me'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I, you and he must attend the party.
You, he and I must attend the party.
He, you and I must attend the party.
You, I and he must attend the party.
questions.explanation: For pleasant/normal plural pronouns, the polite order of persons is 2-3-1: 'You, he and I'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: You, he and I made the mistake.
I, you and he made the mistake.
He, you and I made the mistake.
You, I and he made the mistake.
questions.explanation: When confessing a mistake/blame, the order of persons is 1-2-3: 'I, you and he'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He avails of every opportunity.
He avails himself of every opportunity.
He avails every opportunity.
He is availing of every opportunity.
questions.explanation: 'Avail' is a reflexive verb requiring a reflexive pronoun: 'avails himself of'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He pride on his wealth.
He prides himself on his wealth.
He prides of his wealth.
He is proud on his wealth.
questions.explanation: 'Pride' as a verb takes a reflexive pronoun + 'on': 'prides himself on'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: She enjoyed during the vacation.
She enjoyed herself during the vacation.
She enjoyed in the vacation.
She was enjoyed during the vacation.
questions.explanation: When 'enjoy' has no direct object, a reflexive pronoun is required: 'enjoyed herself'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He absent from the class yesterday.
He absented himself from the class yesterday.
He was absented from the class yesterday.
He had absented from the class yesterday.
questions.explanation: 'Absent' as a verb takes a reflexive pronoun: 'absented himself from'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: I have an urgent business today.
I have urgent business today.
I have some urgent businesses today.
I have an urgent work today.
questions.explanation: 'Business' and 'work' are uncountable nouns; they do not take indefinite article 'an'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He gave me a good advice.
He gave me good advice.
He gave me advices.
He gave me some advices.
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable; cannot take article 'a'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The climate of Ooty is cooler than Coimbatore.
The climate of Ooty is cooler than that of Coimbatore.
The climate of Ooty is cooler than those of Coimbatore.
The climate of Ooty is cooler to Coimbatore.
questions.explanation: Compare climate with climate using 'that of', not climate with the city name.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: The streets of Paris are wider than London.
The streets of Paris are wider than those of London.
The streets of Paris are wider than that of London.
The streets of Paris are wider to London.
questions.explanation: Plural 'streets' requires pronoun 'those of': 'wider than those of London'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Scarcely had he left than the storm began.
Scarcely had he left when the storm began.
Scarcely had he left then the storm began.
Scarcely did he leave than the storm began.
questions.explanation: 'Scarcely had...' is paired with 'when', never 'than'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: No sooner did the train stop when we got down.
No sooner did the train stop than we got down.
No sooner did the train stop then we got down.
No sooner had the train stopped when we got down.
questions.explanation: 'No sooner did...' is paired with 'than', never 'when'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Hardly had she entered the hall than everyone stood up.
Hardly had she entered the hall when everyone stood up.
Hardly had she entered the hall then everyone stood up.
Hardly did she enter the hall than everyone stood up.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly had...' takes 'when'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: Between you and I, this plan is flawed.
Between you and me, this plan is flawed.
Between you and myself, this plan is flawed.
Between yours and mine, this plan is flawed.
questions.explanation: Preposition 'between' takes objective case 'me'.

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is older than me.
He is older than I am.
He is elder than me.
He is elder than I.
questions.explanation: Formal comparative comparison takes subjective case with auxiliary: 'older than I am' (or 'older than I').

questions.question: Identify the correct sentence:
options: He is junior to all his colleagues.
He is junior than all his colleagues.
He is junior from all his colleagues.
He is more junior than all his colleagues.
questions.explanation: 'Junior' takes preposition 'to'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He has been living here since five years.
He has been living here for five years.
He is living here since five years.
He lives here since five years.
questions.explanation: Duration of time ('five years') requires 'for', not 'since'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: I prefer tea than coffee.
I prefer tea to coffee.
I prefer tea over coffee.
I prefer tea more than coffee.
questions.explanation: 'Prefer' takes the preposition 'to'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: She is senior than me.
She is senior to me.
She is senior from me.
She is senior over me.
questions.explanation: Latin comparatives ending in -ior (senior, junior, superior) take 'to'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He walked fastly to catch the train.
He walked fast to catch the train.
He walked fastly for catching train.
He walked more fast to train.
questions.explanation: 'Fast' is both an adjective and an adverb; 'fastly' does not exist in standard English.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is suffering with fever.
He is suffering from fever.
He suffers with fever.
He is suffered from fever.
questions.explanation: 'Suffering' takes the preposition 'from'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Each of the boys have a pen.
Each of the boys has a pen.
Each boys have a pen.
Each of boys are having pen.
questions.explanation: 'Each of' is followed by a plural noun and a singular verb ('has').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: One of my friend is a doctor.
One of my friends is a doctor.
One of my friends are a doctor.
One of my friend are doctor.
questions.explanation: 'One of' takes plural noun ('friends') and singular verb ('is').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He told to me a story.
He told me a story.
He said me a story.
He told that a story to me.
questions.explanation: 'Tell' is a transitive verb that takes an indirect object directly without 'to' ('told me').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: I have received your letter yesterday.
I received your letter yesterday.
I had received your letter yesterday.
I was received your letter yesterday.
questions.explanation: Past time adverbials ('yesterday') strictly require Simple Past ('received'), not Present Perfect.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He died from cancer.
He died of cancer.
He died with cancer.
He died by cancer.
questions.explanation: Direct cause of disease takes 'died of cancer'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Neither he nor his friends was present.
Neither he nor his friends were present.
Neither he or his friends were present.
Neither he nor his friends is present.
questions.explanation: Verb agrees with the nearer subject ('friends' -> 'were').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The sceneries of Kashmir are captivating.
The scenery of Kashmir is captivating.
The sceneries of Kashmir is captivating.
The scenery of Kashmir are captivating.
questions.explanation: 'Scenery' is an uncountable noun with no plural form; takes singular verb 'is'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: She bought two dozens apples.
She bought two dozen apples.
She bought two dozens of apples.
She bought two dozen of apples.
questions.explanation: When preceded by a numeral, 'dozen' remains singular ('two dozen apples').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He gave me many advices.
He gave me much advice.
He gave me many advice.
He gave me an advice.
questions.explanation: 'Advice' is uncountable; use 'much advice' or 'pieces of advice'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The furnitures in the room were old.
The furniture in the room was old.
The furnitures in the room was old.
The furniture in the room were old.
questions.explanation: 'Furniture' is an uncountable singular noun; takes 'was'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He goes to school by foot.
He goes to school on foot.
He goes to school with foot.
He goes to school through foot.
questions.explanation: Idiom for walking is 'on foot', not 'by foot'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: I am knowing the answer.
I know the answer.
I have known the answer now.
I am known the answer.
questions.explanation: Stative verbs like 'know' are not used in continuous tenses.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is having three cars.
He has three cars.
He had been having three cars.
He is have three cars.
questions.explanation: 'Have' denoting possession is stative and cannot take continuous form.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is fond to play chess.
He is fond of playing chess.
He is fond with chess.
He is fond for playing chess.
questions.explanation: 'Fond' takes 'of' followed by a gerund ('fond of playing').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: I look forward to meet you.
I look forward to meeting you.
I look forward meeting you.
I look forward for meeting you.
questions.explanation: Phrasal expression 'look forward to' takes a gerund ('meeting').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: No sooner he arrived than the rain started.
No sooner did he arrive than the rain started.
No sooner had he arrived when the rain started.
No sooner he had arrived than rain started.
questions.explanation: Inversion is required after sentence-initial negative adverb 'No sooner did he arrive than...'

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Hardly I entered the room when phone rang.
Hardly had I entered the room when the phone rang.
Hardly had I entered the room than phone rang.
Hardly did I enter the room then phone rang.
questions.explanation: 'Hardly had I entered... when...'

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Unless you do not apologize, I will punish you.
Unless you apologize, I will punish you.
Unless you will apologize, I punish you.
Unless you didn't apologize, I punish you.
questions.explanation: 'Unless' inherently contains a negative meaning; adding 'not' creates an erroneous double negative.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is comparatively better today.
He is comparatively good today.
He is comparatively more better today.
He is comparatively best today.
questions.explanation: 'Comparatively' already implies comparison; pairing it with comparative degree 'better' is redundant.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Please return back my book.
Please return my book.
Please return again my book.
Please give return my book.
questions.explanation: 'Return' already means 'give back'; using 'back' is redundant.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He entered into the room quietly.
He entered the room quietly.
He entered inside the room quietly.
He entered to the room quietly.
questions.explanation: 'Enter' as physical entry does not take 'into' (only abstract entry takes into: 'enter into an agreement').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: We discussed about the problem for hours.
We discussed the problem for hours.
We discussed on the problem for hours.
We discussed of the problem.
questions.explanation: 'Discuss' is a transitive verb taking a direct object; 'about' is redundant.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: She ordered for two cups of coffee.
She ordered two cups of coffee.
She ordered to two cups of coffee.
She ordered of two cups of coffee.
questions.explanation: 'Order' takes a direct object without preposition 'for'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He resembles to his father.
He resembles his father.
He resembles with his father.
He is resembling his father.
questions.explanation: 'Resemble' does not take a preposition.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He died with his country.
He died for his country.
He died to his country.
He died by his country.
questions.explanation: Dying on behalf of an ideal or nation takes 'died for'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The cat jumped on the table.
The cat jumped upon the table.
The cat jumped in the table.
The cat jumped into the table.
questions.explanation: Movement onto a surface is best expressed by 'upon' or 'onto'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is confident to win.
He is confident of winning.
He is confident for winning.
He is confident in winning.
questions.explanation: 'Confident' takes 'of' + gerund.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is capable to do it.
He is capable of doing it.
He is capable for doing it.
He is capable in doing it.
questions.explanation: 'Capable' takes 'of' + gerund.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: She gave me an useful advice.
She gave me a useful piece of advice.
She gave me useful advices.
She gave me an advice.
questions.explanation: 'Useful' starts with consonant glide /juː/ taking 'a', and 'advice' is uncountable.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He has been absent since Monday.
He has been absent from Monday.
He is absent since Monday.
He was absent since Monday.
questions.explanation: 'Since' is used with a point in time in perfect tenses.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: It is high time we start the work.
It is high time we started the work.
It is high time we will start work.
It is high time to started work.
questions.explanation: 'It is high time + subject' strictly requires the subjunctive Simple Past tense ('started').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: I wish I was a bird.
I wish I were a bird.
I wish I am a bird.
I wish I will be a bird.
questions.explanation: Unreal conditional / wish takes subjunctive 'were'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He behaves as if he was the master.
He behaves as if he were the master.
He behaves as if he is master.
He behaves as if he had been master.
questions.explanation: 'As if' expressing hypothetical unreal state takes 'were'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Though he worked hard but he failed.
Though he worked hard, he failed.
Though he worked hard yet but he failed.
Although he worked hard but failed.
questions.explanation: 'Though' is never paired with 'but'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is the tallest of the two boys.
He is the taller of the two boys.
He is taller of two boys.
He is more tall of two boys.
questions.explanation: When comparing precisely two persons or items, use the comparative degree with 'the' ('the taller').

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Iron is more useful than any metal.
Iron is more useful than any other metal.
Iron is the most useful of any metal.
Iron is more useful of all metals.
questions.explanation: Exclusion of the subject being compared requires 'any other metal'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: She is more cleverer than her sister.
She is cleverer than her sister.
She is most cleverer than sister.
She is more clever than her sister.
questions.explanation: Double comparative ('more cleverer') is grammatically incorrect.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The population of Mumbai is greater than Delhi.
The population of Mumbai is greater than that of Delhi.
The population of Mumbai is greater than Delhi's people.
The population of Mumbai is more than Delhi.
questions.explanation: Comparison must compare like with like: population with 'that of Delhi'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The climate of Kochi is better than Chennai.
The climate of Kochi is better than that of Chennai.
The climate of Kochi is better than Chennai's.
Both B and C are correct.
questions.explanation: Both 'that of Chennai' and possessive 'Chennai's' correctly compare climate to climate.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He has left for London yesterday.
He left for London yesterday.
He had left for London yesterday.
He was left for London yesterday.
questions.explanation: Specific past time 'yesterday' mandates Simple Past 'left'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: I am suffering with cold.
I am suffering from a cold.
I suffer with a cold.
I am having cold.
questions.explanation: 'Suffering from a cold' is the idiomatic expression.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: Divide the property among two brothers.
Divide the property between the two brothers.
Divide the property with two brothers.
Divide the property within two brothers.
questions.explanation: Two entities require 'between'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The cattle is grazing in the meadow.
The cattle are grazing in the meadow.
The cattles are grazing in the meadow.
The cattles is grazing in the meadow.
questions.explanation: 'Cattle' is a plural noun without 's' and takes plural verb 'are'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: The police is investigating the case.
The police are investigating the case.
The polices are investigating the case.
The police has investigating.
questions.explanation: 'Police' is a plural noun taking plural verb 'are'.

questions.question: Spot the correct sentence:
options: He is guilty for theft.
He is guilty of theft.
He is guilty with theft.
He is guilty in theft.
questions.explanation: 'Guilty' takes the preposition 'of'.

questions.question: Find the error / Choose the correct sentence: 'He is my cousin brother.'
options: He is my cousin brother.
He is my cousin.
He is my brother cousin.
He is my cousin sister.
questions.explanation: Rule 23: Do not use 'brother' or 'sister' with 'cousin' when the pronoun 'He' or 'She' already specifies the gender. Correct: 'He is my cousin.'

questions.question: Find the error / Choose the correct sentence: 'She is my cousin sister.'
options: She is my cousin sister.
She is my cousin.
She is my female cousin sister.
She is cousin to me sister.
questions.explanation: Since 'She' already conveys feminine gender, adding 'sister' to 'cousin' is superfluous. Correct: 'She is my cousin.'

questions.question: Spot the correct usage of cousin:
options: I went to the temple with my cousin sister.
He introduced his cousin brother.
She visited her cousin brother.
He met his cousin brother in town.
questions.explanation: When gender is NOT already indicated by subject pronoun (e.g., 'I went with my cousin sister'), specifying gender with sister is acceptable in descriptive context.

questions.question: Identify the incorrect sentence with redundant noun:
options: It was a major blunder.
It was a blunder mistake.
It was a serious error.
It was a costly mistake.
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Blunder' itself means a serious or stupid mistake. Saying 'blunder mistake' is a tautology (redundant nouns).

questions.question: Correct the error: 'The angry mob attacked the police officers.'
options: The furious mob attacked...
The angry crowd attacked...
The mob attacked the police officers.
The angry group attacked...
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Mob' inherently denotes a riotous, angry crowd of people. Prefixing 'angry' is superfluous redundancy. Correct: 'The mob attacked the police officers.'

questions.question: Correct the error: 'He is a coward person.'
options: He is a coward person.
He is a coward.
He is coward man.
He is person coward.
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Coward' is a noun; combining two nouns 'coward person' is incorrect. Say 'He is a coward' or 'He is a cowardly person' (adjective + noun).

questions.question: Choose the correct expression: 'What is the ______ marks in Mathematics?'
options: pass
passing
passed
passable
questions.explanation: Rule 23: Standard English and PSC examination rules dictate 'pass marks', not 'passing marks'.

questions.question: Choose the correct expression: 'Which is the ______ road to the city center?'
options: link
linking
linked
links
questions.explanation: Rule 23: Standard idiom is 'link road', not 'linking road'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'Please put your ______ on the official document.'
options: sign
signature
signed
signing
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Sign' is primarily a verb; the formal noun for one's written name is 'signature'.

questions.question: Choose the correct form: 'Attach your recent ______ to the application form.'
options: photo
photograph
photos
photography
questions.explanation: Rule 23: In formal usage, a physical image attached to paper documents is a 'photograph'.

questions.question: Spot the correct term: 'Beware of the ______ in the crowded train.'
options: pickpocket
pickpocketer
pocket-picker
pick-pocketsman
questions.explanation: Rule 23: The person who steals from pockets is a 'pickpocket' (Verb + Noun compound), not 'pickpocketer'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence regarding building material:
options: The house is made of bricks.
The house is made of brick.
The house is made by bricks.
The house is constructed with bricks.
questions.explanation: Rule 23: When used as material noun, 'brick' remains in singular ('made of brick', just like 'made of stone').

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence regarding tools and apparatus:
options: I have bought all the required equipments.
I have bought all the required equipment.
I have bought all the required equipmentes.
I have bought all equipments.
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Equipment' is an uncountable mass noun with no plural 'equipments'.

questions.question: Choose the correct sentence regarding military staff:
options: The flight was carrying army personnels.
The flight was carrying army personnel.
The flight was carrying army personnels staff.
The flight was carrying army persons.
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Personnel' is an intrinsically plural noun denoting staff or employees; it does not take 's'.

questions.question: Choose the correct word: 'The government ______ did not pay heed to his memorandum.'
options: authority
authorities
authoritative
authorization
questions.explanation: Rule 23: 'Authority' refers to power or jurisdiction; 'authorities' (plural) refers to the persons in power who govern.
